title: Detection of Mail Protocol-Based C2 Activity (SMTP, IMAP, POP3)
shortTitle: Detection of Mail Protocol-Based C2 Activity (SMTP, IMAP,...
summary: Mail protocol command and control (T1071.003) covers controller traffic that rides on the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, the Internet Message Access Protocol, or the Post Office Protocol, because those ports are allowed outbound almost everywhere and are rarely inspected in depth. This detection strategy combines two views: endpoint connection records that attribute a mail protocol session to a process which is not a mail client, and network or proxy records that show repeated short sessions to a mail server the organisation does not own. The features that separate command and control from real mail are regularity of timing, small and consistent payload sizes, long lived sessions with periodic keepalives, and a destination absent from the mail infrastructure inventory. The strategy fails because encryption hides content, because notification services and monitoring appliances generate similar traffic, and because an attacker who uses the organisation's own cloud mailbox is indistinguishable from normal mail at the network layer.

beginner.definition: Email travels using three main protocols. The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol sends mail, and the Internet Message Access Protocol and the Post Office Protocol fetch it. Attackers can hide their control traffic inside these protocols. A command from the attacker looks like an ordinary email. This detection looks for mail traffic that does not come from a mail program.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most networks allow mail traffic to leave, because work depends on it. Security tools often skip deep checks on mail ports for the same reason. So an attacker can send orders to a victim inside messages that look harmless. The traffic reaches a mail server that the attacker controls. This detection helps you find a control channel that hides in plain sight.
howItWorks: Endpoint records show which program opened each network connection.
The rule checks whether the destination port belongs to a mail protocol.
It notes the process image, such as a browser, a script host, or an unknown program.
It measures the timing, the size, and the repetition of each session.
It compares the destination with the list of mail servers your company owns.
An analyst then reviews the mailbox or the server to confirm what happened.
beginner.example: Think of a factory where staff may post letters at any time. The post box is emptied every day, so letters are completely normal. A spy learns this and starts sending instructions in plain looking letters to a friend outside. The letters pass the gate without trouble, because the gate staff only count envelopes. This detection is the guard who asks why a machine in the basement is posting twenty letters an hour. The letters look harmless, but the sender does not belong there.
takeaways: Mail ports are usually open, which is exactly what makes them useful to an attacker.
Compare the sending program with the protocol, not the port on its own.
Regular small sessions to an unknown mail server deserve a closer look.

objectives: Explain why mail protocols are attractive carriers for command and control traffic.
Identify the endpoint and network telemetry that attributes a session to a process.
Recognise timing and payload patterns that differ from a normal mail client.
Compare session destinations against the inventory of mail servers the organisation owns.
Describe how mailbox level evidence can confirm a suspected channel.
dataSources: Sysmon event 3 network connection records for TCP ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995 with process image and destination address
Proxy or secure web gateway logs showing mail protocol sessions originating from workstation subnets
Network flow records with session duration, packet counts, and byte counts for mail protocol ports
DNS query logs for mail exchange records and for mail server hostnames that are new to the environment
logic: Mail protocol command and control is detected by contrasting the protocol in use with the process and the destination, never by inspecting message content. The rule selects outbound sessions on mail ports, removes those opened by known mail clients or internal relays, then scores what remains on three features. The first is the process image, which is usually a script host, a browser, or an unrecognised binary rather than a mail client. The second is the destination, which does not appear in the inventory of mail servers the organisation owns or rents. The third is rhythm, which shows short repeated sessions of similar size at regular intervals instead of the bursty pattern of genuine mail synchronisation. The fields to correlate are the process identifier and image, the destination address and port, the byte counts in each direction, and the interval between sessions. The benign case is a notification service, a monitoring agent, or a scanner appliance sending mail through an internal relay or an approved cloud provider, and those stay stable in destination and volume across weeks.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Non mail process opening a mail protocol connection
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 3
#     DestinationPort:
#       - 25
#       - 465
#       - 587
#       - 993
#       - 995
#   filter_mail_clients:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\outlook.exe'
#       - '\thunderbird.exe'
#   condition: selection and not filter_mail_clients
# level: high
falsePositives: Monitoring and backup appliances that send alert mail through an external provider instead of the internal relay
Application servers that send notification mail straight to a cloud mail service on port 587
Printers and multifunction devices configured to email scanned documents to an external address
Development or test scripts that exercise mail sending against a public test mail service
A browser extension that checks a personal webmail account over a mail protocol port
tuningNotes: Build the inventory of mail servers and relays your organisation owns or rents, plus the internal hosts allowed to speak mail protocols directly, and filter on that inventory rather than on process name alone, because a binary can be named after a mail client. Scope the rule to workstation and application server subnets and leave the mail relay subnet out of it. Require either a non standard process or a non inventory destination before alerting, and set a repetition threshold so a single one off session is not enough. Narrowing this way loses visibility into command and control through a legitimate cloud mailbox, so pair the rule with mailbox audit logging and with detection on unusual mail forwarding rules or folder access.
